answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for a cluster/account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (resource name is the Cosmos DB account).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create an account (MongoDB API): az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. This is in the builtin az cosmosdb group, not an external extension.

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (specify apiProperties or kind=MongoDB). Example Bicep: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: accountName ... }. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (set kind = "MongoDB" and appropriate capabilities).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: MongoDB-style URI. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@myaccount@. TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true or tls=true) and port is 10255 for the Cosmos/MongoDB endpoint.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is typically expressed and billed in Request Units (RU/s) when using Azure Cosmos DB accounts. There is also a serverless mode for low-volume workloads. (Historically Cosmos uses RU model rather than vCore billing for the MongoDB-compatible accounts.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: MongoDB drivers authenticate with username/password (SCRAM credentials created on the account) via the connection string. Cosmos DB also has primary keys for the account. Azure AD (Microsoft Entra ID) data-plane authentication is not generally supported for the MongoDB wire protocol — drivers should use the MongoDB credentials embedded in the URI. (So do not expect integrated Entra ID auth via the MongoDB driver.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., the Node.js mongodb driver or Mongoose). There is no separate MongoDB-specific Azure SDK for applications talking the MongoDB wire protocol — use the official MongoDB client libs with the Cosmos/Mongo connection string.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Expected/typical index types (in this environment) are HNSW and IVF (and DiskANN for disk-backed ANN). In a MongoDB-compatible cluster you create a vector index with a createIndex call on the collection; example (syntactic form I would use): db.orders.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'vec_idx', dimensions: 1536, indexType: 'HNSW', similarity: 'cosine' } ).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text: create MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' }, { default_language: 'english' })) or use the cloud provider's search integration (e.g., Azure Cognitive Search) for richer capabilities. Hybrid (text + vector) is done by combining a vector nearest-neighbour stage with subsequent text filtering/scoring in your application or aggregation pipeline (vector search stage to retrieve candidates, then text-based filters/sorting).

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports specific server-version compatibilities (historically 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4 and later adds 5.0/6.0; recent clusters may advertise MongoDB 7.0 compatibility). However not every server feature is implemented — some admin commands, server-side JavaScript ($where), certain aggregation stages and some GridFS or server-local file operations may be unsupported or limited. Transactions are supported depending on the compatibility version with some throughput/semantic differences.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Two practical options: 1) Use the official MongoDB Docker image for local dev: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7.0 and target mongodb://localhost:27017. 2) Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator if you need Cosmos-specific behaviour (if your local environment supports it). For the live Cosmos Mongo endpoint, the TLS port is 10255.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are supported only when the account's MongoDB compatibility/version and service tier support them. On Cosmos/Mongo accounts you may need a compatible server version (>=4.0/4.2 depending on implementation) and sometimes enable features or set the account to a compatible API version. If unavailable, use Cosmos DB's native change feed as an alternative.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: There is a service-specific MCP server named documentdb (the prompt mentions a 'documentdb' MCP server). For DocumentDB/Cosmos data-plane ops you should use the documentdb MCP server’s tools; the generic Azure MCP server will not provide the same service-specific data-plane inspection tools.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft used the name DocumentDB for the original document database service which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (rebrand/unification of multiple APIs). Azure Cosmos DB is the multi-model, globally distributed service; the term DocumentDB is legacy and also confusingly used in other contexts. This is not the same as unrelated open-source projects named DocumentDB — the Azure offering is the managed Cosmos DB product with a MongoDB-compatible API layer.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary storage/engine exposing a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol. That means most application code can use standard MongoDB drivers unchanged, but some server-side behaviors, limits and unsupported admin operations differ (so test for any advanced MongoDB features your app relies on).

answers.question: Which database name should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_retail_18 for all collections created and read by the sample.

answers.question: How should the Node.js sample connect with Mongoose using the provided environment variable?
answers.answer: Read the full MongoDB URI from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to mongoose.connect, ensuring TLS is enabled. Example: await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { tls: true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: false, retryWrites: false, serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000 }); The URI should already include username/password and host (account.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255).

answers.question: What indexes will the sample create for the returns workflow?
answers.answer: Create a compound index for fast lookups: db.returns.createIndex({ orderId: 1, customerId: 1, status: 1 }); Also create a vector index on the embedding field for nearest-neighbour retrieval: db.orders.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'orders_embedding_idx', dimensions: 1536, indexType: 'HNSW' }).

answers.question: How will agents authenticate to fetch/write documents in this sample?
answers.answer: Agents in the Node.js orchestration will use the single Mongoose connection (configured from DOCUMENTDB_URI). The URI contains the Mongo credentials; no Entra ID token flow is required for the MongoDB driver in this sample.

answers.question: What aggregation/operation will be used to load the order before running policy and refund logic?
answers.answer: Use a simple findOne by orderId in the sample_retail_18.orders collection, e.g. const order = await Orders.findOne({ orderId: requestedOrderId }).lean(); then pass that plain JS object to the policy and refund calculation agents. If doing vector-augmented lookups, use an aggregation pipeline with a vector search stage (e.g., a provider-specific $vectorSearch or createIndex + $sample/nearby stages) to retrieve candidate similar orders.
